title: Co-founder conflict: how too little or too much conflict kills startups, and how to fix it
summary: Garry Tan explains how avoiding conflict with his Posterous co-founder led him to quit in 2010, and how to spot and fix both too little and too much co-founder conflict. Fixes include resolving disagreements on the spot, assigning one owner per area, listening with steel-manning, and getting coaches and trusted advisors involved early.

principles.text: Don't perform a good co-founder relationship; actually build one. Avoiding conflict to look harmonious backfires.
principles.quote: don't make it look like a good startup or a good co-founder relationship spend time actually making it a good startup and actually a good co-founder relationship

principles.text: When you disagree with a co-founder, stay in the room until it's resolved, even if it means cancelling your weekend for a retreat.
principles.quote: if you don't agree on something don't leave the room until you have a resolution if an hour is not enough cancel your weekend go on a hike even go camping get out of dodge have a retreat

principles.text: Don't sacrifice what you know is right for harmony; give more feedback and make sure you're heard.
principles.quote: you can't sacrifice what you know to be right in order to get that harmony early you've got to fight don't swallow your words if you have a point make sure you are heard

principles.text: Constant fighting usually means unclear roles. List every business area and assign exactly one accountable owner to each.
principles.quote: make a list of all the areas needed for your business then figure out who's best at each part and assign one person to it

principles.text: The owner gathers feedback, then makes the call; everyone agrees to disagree and commit, so you stop refighting decisions and move fast.
principles.quote: the owner makes the call and when the call is made everyone agrees to disagree and commit that way you're not fighting the same battles over and over

principles.text: Hire an executive coach early and bring in trusted investors, advisors and founder friends; don't cheap out when your company is on the line.
principles.quote: third-party help when you're at an intractable state can literally save your startup
